content: A septic abortion is defined as an abortion, whether spontaneous or induced, that is complicated by an infection of the upper genital tract, such as endometritis or parametritis. The cornerstone of treatment for septic abortion involves the use of antibiotics, either as a standalone therapy or in combination with procedures to evacuate retained products of conception. Broad-spectrum antibiotic regimens are commonly recommended for managing this condition. However, there is no established consensus on which specific antibiotics or combinations of antibiotics are most effective for treating septic abortion. This review was conducted to address this gap in knowledge and provide evidence to guide clinical practice and policy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of different antibiotics or antibiotic regimens in the treatment of septic abortion. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and POPLINE, using keywords such as abortion, septic abortion, antibiotics, infected abortion, and postabortion infection. Additional searches were performed in the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov for ongoing trials as of April 19, 2016. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-RCTs that compared one antibiotic to another, regardless of the route of administration, dosage, or duration. Studies that compared antibiotics alone to antibiotics combined with other interventions, such as dilation and curettage (D&C), were also considered. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, with disagreements resolved through consultation with a third author. The extracted data were entered into Review Manager 5.3 and cross-checked for accuracy. The review included three small RCTs involving a total of 233 women, all conducted more than 30 years ago. One study compared clindamycin to a combination of penicillin and chloramphenicol. The results showed no significant difference between the two regimens in reducing fever, as measured by the fever index, which quantifies the total amount of fever above a baseline temperature of 99°F (37.2°C). The mean difference (MD) in fever reduction was ‐12.30 (95% confidence interval [CI] ‐25.12 to 0.52), based on data from 77 women in one study. The quality of evidence for this finding was moderate. Similarly, there was no difference in the duration of hospitalization between the two groups, with both groups having a mean hospital stay of 5 days (MD 0.00, 95% CI ‐0.54 to 0.54). Another study compared the combination of penicillin and chloramphenicol to cephalothin and kanamycin, both before and after D&C. The response to therapy was assessed by the time to fever resolution and the time to becoming afebrile after D&C. The evidence, which was of low quality, suggested no significant difference in fever reduction between the two regimens (MD ‐2.30, 95% CI ‐17.31 to 12.71) or in outcomes when D&C was performed during antibiotic therapy (MD ‐1.00, 95% CI ‐13.84 to 11.84). This study involved 56 women. A third study, which had an unclear risk of bias, compared tetracycline combined with enzymes to intravenous penicillin G. The results indicated that tetracycline plus enzymes significantly reduced the time to fever resolution (MD ‐5.03, 95% CI ‐5.77 to ‐4.29) and the time to resolution of leukocytosis (MD ‐4.88, 95% CI ‐5.98 to ‐3.78) compared to penicillin G. This study included 100 women. Treatment failure and adverse events were rare across all studies, and no statistically significant differences were observed between treatment groups. In conclusion, the evidence does not strongly support the superiority of intravenous clindamycin over penicillin plus chloramphenicol for treating septic abortion. Similarly, there is no evidence to suggest that penicillin plus chloramphenicol is more effective than cephalothin plus kanamycin. Tetracycline combined with enzymes appeared to be more effective than intravenous penicillin G in reducing the time to fever resolution, but this finding is based on a single study with a low risk of bias. Overall, the evidence is limited and outdated, as the included studies were conducted over 30 years ago. There is an urgent need for high-quality RCTs to provide reliable evidence on the effectiveness of currently used antibiotics for treating septic abortion. Future research should also focus on including institutions in low-resource settings, such as sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean, and South Asia, where the burden of abortion-related complications is high and healthcare systems face significant challenges.
